exp.0:8:
This verse says that this verse tells the believing brother who is of humble condition, poor or unimportant in the world, to rejoice and take pride in his high spiritual standing. The phrase about a lowly lot describes a humble situation, and the word about boasting means he should be glad and feel honored.

James, writing to Jewish Christians scattered abroad and tested by hardships, has just spoken about asking for wisdom in faith without doubting. Now he turns to poverty and wealth. The verses that follow show that the rich man too must consider his true condition, since riches pass away like the flower of the grass.

For today: if you feel undervalued because of your money, your work or your position, remember that God sees you as his child. Your worth does not depend on what you have, but on what Christ has given you.
exp.0:21:
James says that it is not enough to hear God's Word; it must be practiced. "Doers" are those who carry it out, and "hearers" are those who only listen to it. Whoever only hears deceives himself, that is, he believes he is right with God, but he is mistaken.

James writes to scattered believers, and tradition identifies him with James, the brother of the Lord, although some debate that point. He has just asked them to receive with humility the Word planted in them. Now he clarifies that truly receiving it means obeying it. In the verses that follow, he compares it to looking in a mirror and forgetting what one saw.

For today: after reading the Bible or listening to a teaching, choose one concrete thing you can put into practice that same day, such as forgiving someone, helping someone in need, or speaking with more gentleness. Ask God for strength to do it.
exp.0:24:
This verse speaks of the person who looks carefully into God's perfect law, the law that gives freedom, and does not turn away from it. They are not someone who hears and then forgets, but someone who obeys. God will bless them in what they do. The word "blessed" in the verse means happy or favored, and a "hearer" is simply someone who listens.

James, probably the brother of Jesus and a leader of the church in Jerusalem, writes to believers who are scattered. He warns them that hearing the Word is not enough. Earlier he compared the person who only hears to someone who looks at their face in a mirror and forgets what they look like. Then he gives concrete examples: keeping control of the tongue, and caring for orphans and widows.

For today: after reading or listening to the Bible, choose one specific thing you can practice this week, such as forgiving someone or helping a person in need, and do it.
exp.1:5:
James tells his readers that they have treated the poor with contempt. Then he asks them a question about something they experience themselves: the rich oppress them, that is, they mistreat them by abusing their power, and it is the rich who drag them before the judges, that is, take them there by force.

James writes to Christian believers and corrects a mistake in their congregation: giving good treatment to the rich and bad treatment to the poor. He has just said that God chose the poor to be rich in faith. His argument is that favoring the powerful is unjust and also unwise. Scholars do not know exactly which court cases he had in mind.

Today we can examine how we treat people. Do we give better attention to whoever benefits us or impresses us? This week, greet and listen with the same respect to someone humble and without influence.
exp.1:7:
James says that if you truly keep the royal law, which is loving your neighbor as yourself, as the Scripture teaches, you do well. The verb forms in the quoted phrase are not needed here, and I have omitted the sentences that explained them. The law is called royal because it comes from the King, or because it is the chief law of God's kingdom. This quotation comes from Leviticus 19:18.

James, a leader in the early church, writes to Christians who treated the rich better and looked down on the poor. He reminds them that the rich were oppressing them, and that real love does not show partiality toward persons. The next verse shows that favoritism contradicts that love.

Today, we can ask ourselves whom we treat with the most warmth or respect, and whom we ignore. This week, greet, listen to, or help with the same respect someone you would normally overlook.
exp.1:11:
James asks us that both our words and our actions be those of people who will one day give an account to God.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to scattered Jewish believers. He has just rebuked them for treating the rich better than the poor. He reminds them that the law is a whole: failing at one point, such as favoritism, is to offend against all of it. He then adds that God will show mercy to the one who has shown mercy.

For today: before you speak or act, ask yourself whether what you say and do reflects the mercy you yourself have received. Today, treat with patience and respect someone you would normally ignore or treat harshly.
exp.2:11:
James asks questions using examples from nature. A fig tree does not produce olives, and a vine does not produce figs. Each plant produces according to what it is. In the same way, a spring does not give both salt water and fresh water at once.

James, a leader in the church and a brother in the faith, writes to Christian believers. Earlier he spoke of the power of the tongue: with it we bless God and also curse people. He says this should not be so. Then he goes on to speak of true wisdom, which is shown through a gentle life and good works.

For today: review how you speak at church, at home, and on social media. If you praise God but speak with contempt about others, ask him to cleanse your heart, for words come out of it. Begin with a simple decision: today I will speak with respect and kindness.
exp.2:15:
This verse says that where there is envy and strife, that is, rivalry, quarrels, or selfish ambition, there is also disorder, instability and confusion. In addition, every evil work is produced there, that is, every kind of wickedness and bad deeds.

James, writing as a pastor to scattered Christians, corrects those who boasted of being wise while living with jealousy and rivalry. He tells them that such wisdom does not come from God. He then contrasts that attitude with the wisdom from above, which is pure, peaceable and full of mercy.

Today, before we react with jealousy or competition, we can ask ourselves what is in our heart. If you notice envy toward someone, pray for that person, acknowledge your attitude before God, and look for a word or action that builds peace.
exp.2:17:
He says that righteousness is like a seed that bears fruit, and that this seed grows when it is sown in an atmosphere of peace. Those who work for peace are the ones who harvest a upright and good life. "Fruit of righteousness" means the good works and the right living that please God.

James, who identifies himself as a servant of God and of Jesus Christ and writes to believers scattered abroad, ends here his teaching about true wisdom. Earlier he contrasted envy and quarrels with the wisdom that comes from God, which is pure, peaceable, and full of mercy. This verse sums up that this wisdom produces a good harvest.

Today we can apply it this way: when a conflict arises at home, in the church, or at work, before responding in anger, choose a kind word or take the first step toward reconciliation. In this way you sow something good.
exp.3:0:
James asks where the fights and conflicts among believers come from. He answers himself: they come from desires that are out of order, selfish cravings. These desires wage war within us, in our own inner lives and in the way we act.

The one speaking is James, who writes to Jewish Christians scattered abroad. Tradition identifies him as James, the brother of the Lord, although some debate this point. He writes because there were divisions, envy, and disputes in the communities. He does not first blame others, but the heart.

For today: when a conflict arises in your home, workplace, or church, before pointing at the other person, honestly ask yourself what you are desiring. Bring it to God in prayer and ask him for a humble and peaceful heart.
exp.3:6:
It says we should place ourselves under the authority of God, that is, obey Him and acknowledge Him as Lord. And from that position, resist the devil, that is, not give in to his deceptions, and he will flee away.

James writes to Christians who had quarrels, envy, and pride among them. He has just said that God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble. Therefore, submitting to God is the path of humility. Immediately he invites them to draw near to God and to cleanse their hearts.

For today: when temptation comes, do not fight only with your own strength. First, surrender your pride or your anger to God, pray, and ask Him for help. Then say a firm "no" to whatever you know is pulling you away from Him.
exp.3:16:
This verse says that sin is not only doing what is wrong, but also failing to do good when a person knows they ought to do it. The one who knows what is right is the person who is aware of what is correct. Doing good means acting with justice, love, and obedience to God. Whoever knows it and lets it pass by is at fault.

James, the author of this letter, writes to Christians who were making plans without thinking about God and who boasted about them. He asked them for humility: to recognize that life is brief and that everything depends on the will of the Lord. Then he closes with this principle: knowing what is good brings responsibility. Many understand that it refers mainly to that proud attitude, though the statement applies to everything.

Today we can ask ourselves what good we already know we should do and are putting off: asking for forgiveness, helping someone, or setting aside time for God. Today, take a concrete step and do it with humility.
exp.4:8:
It says that believers should not complain or speak bitterly against one another. "Complain" here means protesting or grumbling with resentment. The phrase about not being condemned means not receiving God's judgment for that attitude. The image of the Judge standing at the door is vivid: he is so near that he could come in at any moment.

James, a leader of the church and, according to Christian tradition, a brother of the Lord, writes to Christians who were facing pressure and hardship. He calls them to be patient until the coming of the Lord, like the farmer who waits for the rain. When the waiting becomes heavy, it is easy to vent frustration on others. James reminds them that God sees everything.

Today, when you are tired or under pressure, before criticizing or blaming someone in your family or your church, stop and pray. Ask God for patience and look for a kind word, remembering that He is the Judge and that He is also merciful.
exp.4:9:
James asks his brothers to look to the prophets as an example. They spoke on God's behalf, and for that reason they suffered, but they endured with patience. "Affliction" means suffering or hardship. "Patience" here means steady endurance, not giving up.

James writes to Christian believers who were going through trials, perhaps injustice and pressure. Earlier he told them to wait for the coming of the Lord and not to complain against one another. Now he gives them real examples of faithful people who also suffered. Afterward he mentions Job as another case.

When you are going through a trial, do not look only at your pain. Think of faithful people in the Bible who kept trusting God. Their story reminds you that suffering does not mean God has abandoned you, and that you can keep going forward with hope.
exp.4:13:
James encourages anyone who is sick to call for the elders of the church, that is, the leaders of the community. They are to pray over the person and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord.

James writes as a pastor to Christian believers and gives practical advice for everyday life: how to speak, how to pray in suffering and in joy. Some understand the oil as a symbol of setting the person apart for God, others as a medicine of the time. The Bible does not fully explain this, so there are several interpretations.

For today: if you are sick, do not spend that time alone. Ask the leaders or brothers and sisters in your church to pray with you, and entrust your health to God with humility.
exp.4:19:
This verse says that whoever helps a sinner turn back from the wrong path saves that person's soul from death and covers many sins. Scholars debate whether "death" refers to eternal spiritual death or to physical and spiritual ruin in this life, and both readings have been defended. There is also debate about whose sins are covered: those of the one who turns away, or those of the one who helps.

James, who writes to scattered Jewish Christians, ends his letter with this call. Earlier he spoke of the prayer of faith and held up Elijah as an example. Now he closes by showing that caring for a brother who strays is part of living out faith.

Today, if you see a brother or sister moving away from God, do not ignore them or judge them harshly. Pray for them, seek them out with humility, and speak to them with kindness and truth, trusting that God is the one who truly restores them.
exp.1:15:
If someone sees a brother or sister with no clothes and no food and only says, "Go in peace, stay warm and well fed," but does not provide for their physical needs, what good is that? The words offer nothing. The verse uses "stay warm and well fed" as a kind wish, and the point is that a wish alone does not meet a real need.

James, who is thought to be the Lord's brother and a leader of the church in Jerusalem, writes to believers. He uses this simple example to show that a faith that stays only in words is empty. He is not teaching that works buy salvation, but that true faith shows itself in acts of love.

Today, if you know someone with a real need, do not stop at saying "I am praying for you." Pray, and also do something concrete: bring food, help with a bill, or give your time.
exp.2:8:
With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people. James points out that the same mouth that praises God can wound those who have been made in God's likeness. "To curse" means to wish harm on someone or to speak of them with contempt. The reference to God's likeness recalls the teaching of Genesis 1:26-27 that human beings were created in the image of God.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to Christian believers. He has just explained that the tongue is hard to control. Now he points out an inconsistency: it makes no sense to worship God and to despise those who bear his image. Scholars debate who James was, but tradition identifies him as the brother of the Lord.

For today: before you criticize, mock, or insult someone, remember that this person has value before God. Make sure your words at home, at work, and on social media are consistent with your prayer and your praise.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that if anyone lacks wisdom, they should ask God for it. He gives generously to everyone, without finding fault. "Ask" means "request it." "Finding fault" means "belittling someone" or "making them feel small for asking." The promise is that this wisdom will be given.

James, who presents himself as a servant of God and of Jesus Christ, writes to believers who were going through trials. He had been speaking about the patience that comes from a tested faith. In the middle of difficulties, we sometimes do not know what to do or how to understand what we are living through, so he encourages them to ask for wisdom. He then adds that it should be asked for in faith, without doubting.

Today, when you face a difficult decision or a problem you do not understand, pray simply and ask God for wisdom. Do not be afraid that he will be angry at your lack of knowledge. He delights in helping his children.
exp.2:13:
If you harbor bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, there is no point in boasting about being wise. Doing so would be denying the truth with your life, claiming to believe one thing while living another. To boast means to brag or show off.

James, who writes as a pastor to scattered believers, had been speaking about the power of words and about consistency: the fig tree does not produce olives, and the spring does not give both sweet and salty water. Earlier he asked who is wise, and answered that it shows in good conduct and gentleness. Here he warns that jealousy and selfish ambition contradict any claimed wisdom.

For today: before boasting of what you know or of your faith, examine your heart. If you feel jealousy at someone's success, bring it to God in prayer and bless that person with a concrete act, such as sincerely congratulating them.
exp.4:2:
Your gold and silver are corroded, and that corrosion will stand as evidence against you. It will consume your flesh like fire. The phrase "hoarded treasure" means gathered and stored up. "The last days" refers to the final times. They stored up treasure when judgment was already near.

James, a leader of the early church, speaks strongly to rich people who were holding back the wages of their workers. His tone resembles that of the prophets of the Old Testament. Interpreters debate whether he was speaking to wealthy believers or to the wealthy in general, but the message is clear: unjust wealth has consequences.

For today: review how you use your money. Pay fairly those who work for you, be generous, and do not place your security in what corrodes. God sees what others overlook.
exp.2:10:
Can both fresh water and salt water flow from the same spring? The obvious answer is no. The spring is the place where the water comes out, and "salt water" here means water that is bitter and unfit to drink.

James, the author of the letter, is writing to believers about the power of the tongue. He has just said that the same mouth blesses God and curses people, who were made in God's likeness. He uses the image of the spring to show that this contradiction is neither natural nor fitting. Many understand it as a call for faith to be consistent.

For today: before you speak, ask yourself whether your words with family, coworkers, or on social media honor God the same way your prayers do. Ask him to make your spring clean.
exp.1:4:
James calls his readers "beloved brothers" and asks them to listen closely. He asks whether God has not chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom he promised to those who love him.

The author is James, who presents himself as a servant of God and of Jesus Christ. He writes to Christians who were treating the rich better than the poor in their gatherings. He reminds them that God does not look at outward appearances. He does not say that all the poor are automatically saved, but that many of them have a rich faith and trust in God.

Today we can examine how we treat people in church and in everyday life. Before giving someone a better place or more attention because of their money or their clothing, let us remember that God values the heart. Let us greet and serve everyone with the same warmth.
exp.3:13:
This verse says that no one knows what will happen tomorrow. Our life is like a mist: it is visible for a moment and then disappears.

James, a leader of the early church, is writing to Christian believers. Earlier he speaks of merchants who plan with complete certainty: they will go to a city, stay for a year, and make money, without taking God into account. James does not forbid planning, but he corrects their pride and their confidence in themselves. Then he invites them to say: "If the Lord wills."

For today: make your plans responsibly, but commit them to God in prayer. Live with humility and gratitude, making good use of today to love and serve.
exp.0:20:
It says that, based on what was already mentioned, we should get rid of all moral filth and every expression of evil. Instead, we are to humbly accept the word that has been planted within us, the word rooted deep inside us. That word can save the soul.

James, a leader of the church and, according to Christian tradition, the brother of the Lord, writes to believers who are scattered. He has just spoken about listening more and getting angry less. Now he invites them to cleanse the heart and receive God's teaching with a teachable spirit. Soon he will say that hearing it is not enough: it must be put into practice.

For today: before reading the Bible, ask God which of your attitudes needs cleansing, such as anger or pride. Then read slowly, with a willingness to obey whatever you discover.
exp.1:0:
James tells his brothers and sisters in the faith not to mix their trust in Jesus Christ with favoritism. "Favoritism" means treating people better or worse based on their appearance, wealth, or social position. Jesus is called "our glorious Lord," which reminds us that He is Lord over all, regardless of their condition.

The writer is James, a Christian leader who addresses believers in a caring, pastoral tone. The verses that follow give an example: in the meeting, the rich person is given a good seat and the poor person is told to stand or stay on his feet. Many believe this James is the brother of Jesus, although the letter itself gives no further details.

Today we can examine how we welcome people in the church and in everyday life. Let us greet the person who arrives poorly dressed with the same warmth and attention as the one who arrives with great wealth or influence.
exp.1:18:
Here James says that believing correctly that God is one is good, but it is not enough. Even the demons believe that, and they shudder, that is, they tremble in fear before God. They know God exists, but that does not change the way they live or bring them closer to Him.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to scattered Jewish believers. He speaks with firmness because some were claiming to have faith but were not helping the needy or living out what they believed. He uses a direct question, almost like a debate, to show that a faith without works is empty. Some understand that this does not contradict Paul, since they are addressing different problems.

For today: do not settle for simply saying "I believe in God." Ask yourself this week: what will my faith make visible? Perhaps forgiving someone, helping someone, or being honest at work.
exp.3:3:
Your Bible calls believers who are unfaithful to God "adulterers and adulteresses," like someone who breaks a promise of love. "The world" here does not mean the created earth, but the way of living that ignores God and is guided by selfishness. Choosing to be a friend of that way of life puts you in opposition to God.

James writes to Christians who were dealing with quarrels, envy, and cravings that divided them. He tells them that their fights come from selfish desires and from asking for things to spend on their own pleasures. After this strong warning, he reminds them that God gives greater grace to the humble and opposes the proud. It is a call to return to Him.

Today, examine which desires are ruling your heart: money, recognition, comfort. Speak honestly with God about where you have drifted, and humbly ask Him to draw you close to Himself again.
exp.1:9:
Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it. That means a person who obeys God's law nearly everywhere but fails in one commandment has already broken the whole law. "Stumbles" means to trip or fall short, and "guilty of breaking all of it" means the person stands as a lawbreaker before the entire law, not just before that one point.

James, the author of this letter, writes to scattered Jewish believers. He warns them against showing partiality, that is, treating the rich better than the poor. Some thought that keeping certain commandments made up for other failings. James shows that the law is a unity, given by one God, and that favoritism is a real act of disobedience.

Today we can avoid saying, "I'm not that bad, I only fail in this one thing." If there is an area where we treat someone with contempt or favoritism, let us recognize it with humility and ask God for his mercy and his help to change.
exp.1:25:
This verse makes a comparison: just as a body without the spirit, meaning without the breath of life, is dead, so a faith that produces no deeds is also dead. "Deeds" means concrete actions that show what a person believes.

James, traditionally identified as the brother of Jesus and a leader of the church in Jerusalem, writes to Christians who said they had faith but did not help those in need. He gives examples such as Abraham and Rahab, whose trust in God was seen in what they did. Some believe this does not contradict Paul, since James speaks of a faith that is shown, not of earning salvation.

Today, saying "I believe in God" is not enough. Think of one concrete action this week, such as visiting someone who is sick or helping a neighbor, so that your faith can be seen in what you do.
exp.2:4:
James compares the tongue to something very small that has great power. Although it is a small part of the body, it can accomplish enormous things, for good or for harm. He says that a small spark can set a great forest ablaze. The tongue "boasts of great things" means that it brags about great achievements, and in fact it achieves them.

James, who according to tradition was the brother of Jesus and a leader of the church in Jerusalem (some scholars debate his exact identity), writes to scattered Jewish Christians. Earlier he used the bit of a horse and the rudder of a ship as examples of small things that steer something large. He wants believers to see that their words are not a minor matter, but reveal the heart and can harm an entire community.

Today, before sending a message, posting something, or commenting about another person, pause and ask yourself: "Does this build up, or could it start a fire?" Ask God to guide your words, as the rudder guides the ship.
exp.1:21:
James says that Abraham's faith and his actions were working together, not separately. "Working with" means that his faith was moving at the same time as what he was doing. "Perfected by what he did" means that his faith reached its full maturity when it showed itself in actions. It does not say that faith is worthless, but that faith is incomplete if it is never lived out.

James, a leader of the church in Jerusalem, writes to scattered Jewish believers. He corrects those who claimed to have faith but did not help anyone. He points to Abraham, who obeyed God when he offered Isaac. Paul speaks of being accepted by God through faith; James speaks of faith that is proven. Many see that the two complement each other.

For today: examine a belief you say you hold, such as trusting God or loving your neighbor, and take one concrete step this week, such as visiting someone, helping, or forgiving.
exp.4:5:
It says that wealthy, unjust people have condemned and even murdered an innocent person, and that this person did not fight back.

James, a leader of the church and brother of the Lord, speaks sharply to rich people who exploited their workers and did not pay them. It is not clear whether "the righteous one" is a specific person, the poor in general, or even Jesus; there are different interpretations. What is clear is that the oppressed had no way to resist, and God sees them.

For today: if you have power over others, treat them justly and pay what is owed. And if you suffer injustice, trust that God sees everything and wait with patience, without seeking revenge.
exp.3:14:
James says that when we make plans, we should remember that we depend on God. "If the Lord is willing" means "if it is his will." "If we live" means "if we remain alive." "We will do this or that" means "we will do such-and-such a thing."

The one speaking is James, a church leader writing to believers. Shortly before, he corrects merchants who planned trips and profits as if they controlled the future. He reminds them that life is brief, like a mist. Then he calls that self-confidence "pride." He does not condemn planning, but doing it without taking God into account.

Today you can make your plans responsibly, but entrust them to God in prayer. Before a project, a trip, or a decision, say sincerely: "Lord, if it is your will." It is not a magic phrase; it is an attitude of humility and trust.
exp.1:22:
It says that what Genesis records about Abraham came fully true: he believed God, and God credited him as righteous. That is why he was called "a friend of God." The word "fulfilled" in the verse above is the one this comment refers to; "credited" means counted to his account, and "righteousness" here means being right before God.

James, a church leader, writes to scattered Jewish believers. He corrects a faith that is only spoken in words. He quotes Genesis 15:6 and links it with Isaac's offering, to show that true faith is seen in what a person does. Paul speaks of being declared righteous by faith; James speaks of how that faith is proven. Some see the two as complementary.

For today: trust God, and let that trust show in a concrete action, such as forgiving, helping, or being honest this week.
exp.1:23:
This verse says that a person is declared righteous before God not only because of what they believe, but also because of what they do. "As you can see" points to the examples James has just given. "Justified" means recognized or declared righteous. James is saying that true faith does not stay only in words.

James is writing to believers and wants to correct an empty faith, one that says it believes but does not change a life. He uses Abraham and Rahab as examples of faith that showed itself through actions. Some think this clashes with Paul, who speaks of being justified by faith. Many understand it this way: Paul speaks of how a relationship with God begins, and James of how real faith looks.

For today: examine whether what you say you believe shows up in your decisions. Today, do one concrete act of love, such as helping someone or forgiving.
exp.1:16:
The verse says that faith which does not result in action is dead. In other words, faith that is not shown through deeds has no life. It is not doing what faith is meant to do. Here the phrase "by itself" means faith standing on its own, with nothing following from it, so that it does not function or bear fruit.

James, a leader in the church and the author of this letter, writes to believers. Earlier he gave the example of someone who is hungry and cold and is only offered kind words. His point is that saying "I have faith" is not enough if there is no practical compassion. Some debate how this relates to Paul's teachings about faith, but James speaks of a faith that is demonstrated.

For today: think of a person close to you who has a real need, such as food, company, or help with something, and do something concrete for them today. In this way your faith becomes visible.
exp.2:2:
When we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we can guide the whole animal. A rider uses a small piece of metal in the horse's mouth, and with it the rider gets the animal to respond and be steered. That small piece directs the whole body of the horse.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to Christian believers. Earlier in his letter he spoke about teachers and about how easy it is to fail with words. Here he uses the bit as a comparison: just as something small steers something large, the tongue has enormous power. He will go on to speak of the rudder of a ship and of a spark that sets a forest on fire.

For today: before you speak when you are upset, pause briefly and pray in silence. Ask God to help you choose words that build up and do not wound. A moment of self-control can guide the whole conversation.
exp.3:15:
What it says: James is speaking about people who boast about their proud intentions and what they plan to achieve. The verse calls this kind of boasting evil, because it acts as though a person controls the future. Here the word "boast" is the key term: it means showing off or bragging, and it names the proud, arrogant attitude behind such talk.

Context: James, a leader in the early church, writes to Christians who were making business plans without thinking about God (vv. 13-15). He reminds them that life is like a mist, brief and fragile. For this reason they should acknowledge that their plans depend on the Lord's will. He does not forbid making plans, but making them with pride and without depending on God.

For today: Before making plans, work, or projects, bring them to prayer. Plan with wisdom, but with humility, recognizing that your time is in God's hands. And when something turns out well, give thanks instead of boasting.
exp.4:0:
James gets the attention of the rich with strong words. The phrase "Come now" is a way of saying "Listen up, pay attention!" He tells them to weep and wail over the misery that is coming upon them: suffering and judgment.

The speaker is James, a leader of the early church, writing to Christian believers. Earlier in the letter he had already condemned showing favoritism toward the rich. Here he speaks with the tone of an Old Testament prophet. He does not say that having money is sinful in itself, but he warns those who trust in their wealth, hoard it, and use it unjustly. Some think he is addressing rich unbelievers; others think he is also giving a warning to the church.

Today we can ask ourselves: what do I trust in more, my money or God? Having possessions is not wrong, but God calls us to be generous and fair to those who work for us and to those in need.
exp.3:1:
This verse says that disordered desires of the heart lead people to fight. "Crave" means wanting something intensely that we do not have. "Covet" describes a strong, burning desire for what belongs to someone else. "Kill" can be understood literally or as extreme hatred; scholars do not fully agree. In the end, James says that something simple is missing: asking God.

James, leader of the church and called the brother of the Lord, writes to scattered Jewish Christians. He speaks to them firmly because there were quarrels and rivalries among them. He shows them that the problem is not outside them, but in their own desires. Then he explains that they do not have what they want because they do not ask God for it.

Today, when you feel envy or anger over something you want, stop and bring it to God in prayer. Sincerely ask Him to examine your motives and give you peace, instead of fighting or competing with others.
exp.0:0:
James calls himself a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, meaning someone who obeys and serves them. He writes to the twelve tribes of the Dispersion, that is, to God's people scattered among many places. The word "Greetings" was a common way to open a letter, much like wishing someone well.

The writer is James, perhaps the brother of Jesus and a leader of the church in Jerusalem, although tradition and scholars debate his exact identity. Some understand the "twelve tribes" to be Jewish believers scattered abroad; others take it to refer to the whole church. He writes to encourage and guide believers who were facing difficulties, as the following verses show.

For today: although James was a respected figure and could have presented himself with important titles, he calls himself a "servant." We can follow his example and serve with humility, without seeking recognition.
exp.4:12:
He says that when someone is going through a hard time, they should pray. And when someone is cheerful, they should sing praises to God. "Suffering" means going through pain or distress. "Praises" are expressions of honor and thanks offered to God.

James writes to Christians who were enduring trials and pressures. Earlier he spoke about having patience and being sincere in what we say. Now he gives a simple guide: in every state of the heart, whether sorrow or joy, we should turn to God. Afterward he goes on to speak about praying for the sick.

For today: do not keep your emotions far from God. When you are distressed, speak to Him honestly in prayer. When something goes well, don't let it pass by: give thanks by singing or praising Him. In this way your daily life stays connected to Him.
exp.0:18:
This verse says that everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger.

James writes to believers whom he calls "my beloved brothers." He has just reminded them that God is good, does not change, and gave us new life through his word of truth. For this reason, James asks for a way of living that responds to that gift. He then explains that human anger does not produce the righteousness of God, and he encourages receiving God's word with humility.

For today: before you respond in a discussion, pause, listen to the end, and pray briefly. This way you will have more calm and more wisdom to speak.
exp.3:2:
This verse says that sometimes we pray and do not receive what we ask for, because we ask with the wrong motives. The word "wrong" here means with mistaken or selfish intentions. "Pleasures" refers to personal enjoyment and desires, and "squander" means using what we receive only to satisfy ourselves.

James, the author of the letter, is writing to believers who were fighting among themselves. He explains that these conflicts come from selfish desires within the heart. A verse earlier he says they did not have because they did not ask, and here he adds that when they did ask, they did so with wrong motives. He then calls them to give up friendship with the world and return to God.

For today: before you pray for something, ask yourself honestly why you want it. Ask God to purify your motives, so that what you request also serves others and brings honor to Him, not only your own comfort.
exp.0:12:
When tempted, no one should say, "God is tempting me." This verse says that when someone feels the pull to do wrong, they should not blame God for it. The reason is that God cannot be drawn toward evil, and he does not tempt anyone to it. Here "tempt" means pushing or pulling someone toward sin.

James, a leader in the early church, writes to believers who were going through hard trials. Earlier he spoke of the trial that strengthens faith and that God rewards. Here he makes a distinction: God allows trials to mature us, but he never pushes us to sin. The source of evil desire, he says next, lies in our own hearts.

For today: when you feel tempted, do not say "God put me in this" or blame others. Honestly acknowledge what you feel, ask God for strength, and move away from whatever makes you fall. He is good and wants to help you.
exp.1:14:
Here James gives the example of a brother or sister in the church who are without clothes and without the food they need for the day. It is a real and urgent need.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to Christian believers. He wants to correct a faith that stays only in words. Earlier he spoke of mercy, and now he uses this everyday scene to ask what good it is to say you have faith if there are no works. The next verse completes the thought.

For today: if you know someone in your church or your neighborhood who is going without, do not stop at good wishes or prayers alone. Ask what they need and help with something concrete, such as groceries, clothing, or transportation.
exp.2:16:
This verse describes what the wisdom that comes from God is like. First it is pure, that is, clean of bad motives. Then it is peace-loving, gentle, and accommodating. "Gentle" here means kind, one who knows how to yield without fighting. "Accommodating" means willing to listen and be persuaded by good reasons. It is full of mercy and good fruit. "Impartial" means free of favoritism, and "sincere" means genuine, without pretending.

James, a leader in the early church, writes to believers who had envy and quarrels among themselves. Before this verse he contrasts human wisdom, which produces disorder, with God's wisdom, which produces peace.

For today: before answering in an argument, ask yourself whether your words seek to win or seek peace. Ask God for a clean heart, and treat others with honesty and kindness, without pretending to be what you are not.
exp.4:4:
These rich people have lived for pleasure and luxury in this world, with no check on their desires. The verse says they have "lived on earth in luxury and self-indulgence," so their comfort was the center of their lives. The image of "fattening your hearts" is like fattening an animal for slaughter: they have filled themselves with comforts. And they have done so "in the day of slaughter," when others were suffering, yet for them life went on as a feast.

James, a leader of the church, writes firmly to rich people who grew wealthy by cheating their workers out of their wages. He warns them that God hears the cry of the oppressed. Many think he is speaking to rich people outside the community, and others think he means some within the community; the text does not make this clear.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our comforts make us indifferent to those who work for us or near us. Paying fairly and living generously is a way of obeying God.
exp.1:8:
It says that treating some people better than others because of their appearance, money, or position is sin. "Showing favoritism" means playing favorites. The word "convicted" means accused or found guilty, and "transgressors" are those who break the law. In other words, God's own law shows that favoritism is a fault.

James, a leader of the church and, according to the New Testament, the brother of the Lord, writes to Jewish believers scattered abroad. Shortly before, he rebuked the practice of honoring the rich and looking down on the poor in their meetings. He reminds them that loving your neighbor as yourself is the "royal law," and that favoritism goes against it.

For today: think about whom you treat with the most courtesy in your church, at work, or in your neighborhood. This week, give the same respect and patience to someone plain or without influence, as Jesus would have done.
exp.3:7:
He says that if we take a step toward God, he also draws near to us. The words "draw near" simply mean to come close. Next he speaks to sinners, telling them to cleanse their hands, that is, to change their conduct. And to the double-minded, the undecided who want to serve God and the world at the same time, he calls for them to purify their hearts, that is, to cleanse their intentions.

James speaks as a church leader to believers who were living amid quarrels, envy, and pride, as the preceding verses show. That is why he reminds them that God gives grace to the humble. Many scholars think this James is the brother of Jesus, though some debate his identity. The call to draw near comes after the request to submit to God and resist the devil.

Today, if you feel distant from God or live divided, come near with sincerity: pray, confess what weighs on you, and decide on one concrete act of obedience this week. God responds to a humble heart.
exp.1:17:
James imagines someone arguing with him. That person says: "You have faith, and I have deeds." Then the author responds: "Show me your faith without deeds, and I will show you my faith by my deeds." In other words, faith cannot be seen unless it is expressed in actions.

James, a Christian leader in the early church, writes to scattered Jewish believers. He has just spoken of someone who wishes peace to a needy brother but gives him no food or clothing. Interpreters debate who exactly speaks in the dialogue, but the central idea is clear: real faith shows in how one lives.

Today, ask yourself: how does my faith show up in practice? This week, look for a specific need near you, and help with something simple.
exp.0:19:
This verse says that when a person becomes angry, that anger does not produce what God considers just and right. The phrase "bring about" points to producing or accomplishing something. Anger, even when it feels justified, is still anger. Even when we believe we are right, our anger does not bring about the results God desires.

James, probably the brother of Jesus and a leader of the church in Jerusalem, writes to scattered believers. He has just said that we should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to get angry. Then he invites them to receive the word of God with humility and to put it into practice, not just hear it.

For today: when something bothers you, before you respond, pause, take a breath, and listen. Ask God for calm. That way your words can build up instead of hurt.
exp.2:1:
James says that all of us stumble in many ways. If someone is never at fault in what he says, that person is "perfect," meaning mature and complete. Here "stumble" means to make a mistake or fall short. That person could also control their whole body, just as a horse is steered with a bit.

The one speaking is James, leader of the church in Jerusalem and perhaps the brother of Jesus (this is how most people understand it, though not everyone does). He has just warned that teachers will be judged more strictly, because teaching means speaking a great deal and with authority. That is why he gives this example: the tongue is small, yet it directs the whole of life, like the bit and the rudder he mentions later.

Today, before you respond in anger, criticize, or boast, pause briefly and ask God to help you choose words that build up. Mastering the tongue begins with small daily restraints.
exp.3:10:
James asks believers to stop slandering one another. Here "slander" means speaking against someone or criticizing them, and "judging" means condemning them as if you were their judge.

He says that whoever does this speaks against God's law and judges it, because the law commands love for one's neighbor. If you look down on that law, you no longer obey it; you put yourself above it as a judge.

James, traditionally identified as the brother of the Lord, writes to Christians who were suffering divisions and quarrels. Just before this, he calls them to humble themselves and repent before God. Then he reminds them that only God gives the law and can save or condemn. Some scholars debate which law he has in mind, but the context points to the law of love.

Today, before saying something negative about someone, ask yourself whether you would say it in front of that person and whether it helps in any way. If not, it is better to stay silent or pray for them.
exp.0:11:
Blessed is the person who perseveres under trial. The word "blessed" means happy and favored. "Person" here refers to anyone, whether a man or a woman. The trial in view is a hardship or difficulty. The phrase "stood the test" means that after enduring, the person comes through approved. The "crown of life" is a reward that God promises to those who love him.

James, probably the brother of Jesus and a leader of the church in Jerusalem, writes to Jewish Christians scattered abroad who were going through poverty and pressure. Earlier he spoke of the rich and the poor, reminding readers that riches fade away. Afterward he makes clear that God does not tempt anyone toward evil. Some understand the crown as eternal life; others understand it as a reward of joy and a full life.

Today, when you face a difficulty, do not lose heart. Ask God for strength to keep trusting him, remembering that he rewards the perseverance of those who love him.
exp.4:18:
James speaks to believers as brothers and sisters. He says that one of them may wander from the truth, that is, drift away from the right path of faith, whether in what they believe or in how they live. And "someone brings him back" means that another believer helps him return to God.

James writes to Christians who were suffering trials and had problems among themselves. He has just spoken about the prayer of faith, and he held up Elijah as an example of an ordinary person whose prayer was powerful. Now he closes the letter with the responsibility to look after one another. The next verse speaks of saving a soul from death; interpreters debate whether this refers to physical or spiritual death.

If you see a brother or sister drifting away, do not criticize them from a distance or ignore them. Pray for them, approach them with humility, and speak to them with love, seeking to bring them back.
exp.4:14:
It says that when the church prays with faith in God for a sick person, God can restore them to health. "Restore" here means heal or relieve, and "will raise him up" refers to the sick person recovering. It also says that if the illness was connected to some sin, God will forgive it. "If he has sinned" does not claim that every illness comes from sin.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to Christians who were suffering trials. He teaches them to pray in every situation: affliction, joy, or sickness. He asks them to call for the elders, who pray and anoint with oil in the name of the Lord. Some understand the oil as a symbol of setting the person apart for God; others understand it as medicine. The Bible does not fully explain this.

Today, if you are sick or know someone who is, do not pray alone: ask brothers and sisters in your church to pray with you, and entrust the outcome to God.
exp.4:11:
James asks believers not to make oaths, whether by heaven, by the earth, or by anything else like them. Instead, let your word be simple: when you say "Yes," let it mean yes, and when you say "No," let it mean no. The judgment he warns about is the result of not doing this, so that you will not come under it.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to Christians who were facing pressure and hardship. He has just spoken about patience in suffering. His teaching resembles that of Jesus in Matthew 5:33-37. Scholars debate whether it forbids every legal oath or condemns the casual and false use of oaths. What is certain is that he calls for complete honesty.

For today: work at being a trustworthy person. Keep what you promise, avoid exaggerating to win others over, and let your life back up your words.
exp.1:24:
James places Rahab as a second example, after Abraham. He says she was "justified by her actions" because she welcomed the spies from Israel and sent them off on another route, to protect them. "Prostitute" is the word the verse uses for her. "Justified" here means her faith was shown to be genuine.

James writes to believers who said they had faith but were not helping anyone. According to Joshua 2, Rahab believed in the God of Israel and acted at the risk of her life. James does not contradict Paul: he speaks of the faith that is proven by deeds. Some scholars explain the word "justified" in different ways, but all see here a living faith.

Today: if you say you trust God, let it show in something concrete. Help someone in need this week, even if it costs you a little.
exp.0:13:
What it says: James explains where temptation comes from. "Evil desires" means strong, twisted longings that push us toward what is wrong. "Lured away" means carried off, like someone who wanders from the path. "Enticed" is a word from fishing: the person is caught with bait. Each person is tempted when their own evil desires pull them along and hook them.

Context: James, traditionally identified as the brother of the Lord and leader of the church in Jerusalem, writes to Christians who are suffering trials. Some could say "God is tempting me" to excuse their fall. He corrects this: God tests to strengthen, but never pushes toward evil. The root of temptation lies within us.

For today: Instead of blaming others or circumstances, honestly recognize which desire makes you fall. Bring it to God in prayer and move away from what is baiting you.
exp.2:5:
James says that the tongue is like a fire that does great harm. It sits among our body parts, yet it can stain and damage a person's whole life. The phrase "sets the course of his life on fire" pictures words spreading destruction through everything a person does. Scholars read this in more than one way, but the core point is clear: the tongue has a serious effect on the whole person. The verse also says the tongue is itself set on fire by hell, meaning its destructive power comes from a source of evil and judgment.

James, a leader in the early church, writes to Christian believers. He wants to show them that words, though they may seem small, have enormous power, like the rudder of a ship or a spark in a forest.

For today: before you speak or write an angry comment, pause and ask God to guide your words. Ask yourself whether what you are about to say builds up or tears down.
exp.2:7:
What it says: James states that no human being can tame the tongue. He calls it a restless evil, meaning it does not easily stay under control, like a wild animal that keeps getting loose. And it is full of deadly poison, since words can wound and destroy, just as the poison of a snake does.

Context: James, writing as a pastor to scattered believers, has just said that people have tamed every kind of animal. He contrasts that with our inability to control what we say. Later he points out the inconsistency of blessing God and cursing people with the same mouth.

For today: before you answer in anger or pass on gossip, pause and pray: "Lord, keep my mouth." Recognizing that we need God's help is the first step toward speaking with respect and kindness.
exp.4:15:
It says that believers should confess their sins to one another and pray for one another, so that there may be healing. It also affirms that the prayer of a righteous person has great power to prevail. "Sins" means wrongs we have done against God or others; "pray" means to ask God in prayer; "healed" may refer to healing of the body, of the soul, or of both; "great power to prevail" means it accomplishes what it asks with strength.

James, a church leader writing to scattered Jewish Christians, had been speaking about prayer for the sick and the forgiveness of sins. Here he widens the idea to the whole community. Then he points to Elijah as an example that the prayer of an ordinary man, with the same weaknesses as we have, was heard.

Find a trusted brother or sister, honestly tell them about a struggle you are carrying, and ask them to pray for you. Do the same when others entrust theirs to you.
exp.0:9:
This verse says that the rich believer should rejoice when he is brought low, that is, when he recognizes that before God he is no more than others. The reason is that the rich man will pass away like a flower of the field: his life and his wealth are brief. Here "low position" means being brought down or having little importance, not something shameful.

James, probably the brother of the Lord, writes to Jewish Christians scattered abroad who were suffering trials. In the verse before, he encouraged the poor brother to glory in his exaltation, his dignity in Christ. Now he tells the rich man that his true worth does not lie in his money either, but in the same thing: Christ.

For today: do not place your identity in what you have or in what you lack. Be thankful for what God has given you, use it generously, and remember that your true worth lies in being a child of God.
exp.1:3:
James asks: if you treat the rich man better and look down on the poor, haven't you divided yourselves inside and become judges with wrong motives? The phrase "have you not discriminated among yourselves" can be understood as "you make distinctions among you" or "you doubt in your hearts." "Evil thoughts" are twisted reasoning that leads people to value others by their outward appearance.

James, one of the leaders of the early church, writes to Christian believers. He corrects them because in their gatherings they gave the best place to the one who seemed important and pushed the poor aside. This contradicted the faith they said they had. Some scholars think this describes a church meeting, and others a kind of internal court; the text allows for both possibilities.

Today, examine how you receive people. Before you judge by clothing, money, or position, ask God to help you see each person with his eyes and to treat each one with the same respect and kindness.
exp.0:16:
It says that every good and perfect thing we receive comes from God, not from ourselves or from chance. The word "gift" in the source means something given freely. "Father of the heavenly lights" probably refers to God as the creator of the sun, the moon and the stars. Unlike them, which change and cast shadows as they move, God does not change: there is no change or shifting shadow in him.

James, a leader of the church and probably the brother of Jesus (as many understand it), writes to believers who are suffering trials. He has just said that sin arises from one's own desire, not from God. So he warns: "do not be deceived." God does not tempt anyone; he gives good things, and by his word he gave us new birth.

Today: when you have doubts or difficulties, remember that God is constant and good. Before you complain, make a list of three gifts you have received and give thanks for them. That strengthens trust in him.
exp.3:4:
James asks whether we think Scripture speaks without reason. The reader's translation says the Spirit God caused to dwell in us yearns with envy. The verse is hard to read. Some take it to mean that our own spirit longs with jealousy and rivalry. Others take it to mean that God himself jealously longs for the Spirit he placed in us. It is also not certain which passage James has in mind.

James, a Christian leader, rebukes believers who were fighting among themselves because of selfish desires. He calls them "adulterers" because they were turning away from God by loving the values of the world. Then he reminds them that God gives greater grace to the humble.

Today, when you feel envy or desires that take over your heart, do not excuse them. Bring them before God with humility and ask him for a simple and grateful heart.
exp.2:6:
This verse says that people have learned to tame every kind of animal: those that walk on land, those that fly, those that crawl, and those that live in the sea. The word "kinds" here refers to the different types of creatures. The phrase "are being tamed and have been tamed" means that people have always been able to control them, and still do.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to believers scattered abroad and teaches them how to live a faith that shows itself in deeds. In this passage he speaks of the power of words. He uses the comparison with animals to prepare the next verse: if people can tame wild animals, it is all the more striking that they cannot tame their own tongue.

For today: before you answer in anger or share a piece of gossip, pause and pray briefly. Ask God for help so that your words bless and do not wound.
exp.0:2:
This verse says that when our faith is put to the test, the result is perseverance. "Knowing" means "understanding" or "being aware of something." A "test" is like an exam that shows whether faith is genuine and firm. "Develops" means "produces" or "builds up." The perseverance here is endurance, the steadiness to keep trusting.

The speaker is James, servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, who writes to Jewish believers scattered in various places. Many were suffering hardships. For this reason he asks them to see trials with joy, since God uses them to form them. Some think this James is a brother of Jesus, although the text does not state this clearly here.

For today: when you go through a difficult time, do not despair or think that God has abandoned you. Ask him for strength to keep trusting one day at a time. Over time, that steadiness will make you firmer.
exp.1:6:
Doesn't James ask whether the wealthy people are the ones who blaspheme the noble name by which you have been called? To blaspheme means to speak with contempt about God or what is sacred. The noble name almost certainly refers to Christ, the name your community was called by, perhaps at baptism, though some understand it in a more general way.

James, a leader of the church and the Lord's brother, writes to scattered Jewish Christians. He rebukes them because they treated the rich better than the poor in their gatherings. He reminds them that the very wealthy, influential people were oppressing them and mocking their faith. We do not know exactly who they were, but the argument is clear: it makes no sense to honor someone who dishonors Christ.

Today, before giving special treatment to someone because of their money or position, ask yourself what Christ values. Treat everyone with equal respect and love.
exp.0:25:
This verse says that if someone thinks they are a religious person, but does not control what they say, they are deceiving their own heart, and their religion is worthless. The word "bridle" means to hold back and restrain, the way a rider controls a horse. "Worthless" means without value, so their religious practice accomplishes nothing.

The one speaking is James, a leader of the early church, who writes to Jewish believers scattered outside their homeland. Tradition identifies him as the brother of Jesus, though some debate this. He has been speaking about being doers of the word and not only hearers. With this verse he shows that true faith is seen in daily conduct, and the next verse speaks of caring for orphans and widows.

For today: before you speak, especially when you are angry or on social media, pause for a moment and ask yourself whether your words help or hurt. Ask God to guide what you say, because the way you speak shows what your faith really is.
exp.3:5:
What it says: God is generous and gives a grace greater than our selfish desires. That is why Scripture says God opposes the proud, that is, the arrogant, but gives grace to the humble.

Context: James, leader of the church and author of the letter, writes to believers who were fighting among themselves out of envy and selfish desires. He calls them to give up friendship with the world, which means living far from God. The quotation appears to come from Proverbs 3:34. He then invites them to submit to God and draw near to him.

For today: When you notice pride, for example when you refuse to ask for forgiveness or help, stop and pray sincerely: "Lord, I need your grace." Recognizing our need opens the door to his help.
exp.3:11:
It says that there is only one Lawgiver and Judge, the One who is able to save and to destroy. That is why James asks, "But who are you to judge your neighbor?" The word "destroy" here means to ruin or condemn. "Judge" refers to criticizing or condemning one's neighbor, not to having discernment.

James, according to tradition the leader of the church in Jerusalem, writes to believers who had quarrels and criticisms among themselves. Earlier he urged them to humility and to stop speaking evil of one another. Afterward he warns them against boasting about the future, because life is brief like a vapor. Both points point toward humility before God.

For today: before criticizing someone, remember that you too depend on the mercy of God. Instead, pray for that person and speak to them with love, leaving the final judgment in God's hands.
exp.0:15:
James tenderly says to them: "Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers." To be deceived here means to be misled, to be tricked into believing something false, or to wander off the right path. It is a loving warning so that no one gets confused about something important.

James, who writes to believers scattered abroad and going through trials, has just explained that evil desire in the heart leads to sin and sin leads to death. So he warns: do not think that God is tempting you. Right away he shows them that only good and perfect gifts come from God, because He does not change.

For today: when temptation comes, do not blame God or your circumstances. Recognize what is happening in your heart, ask God for help, and remember that He is good and wants to give you life.
exp.0:22:
James says that anyone who hears God's word but does not carry it out is like a person who looks at their face in a mirror. To "carry it out" means to obey, to put what was heard into practice. "Face as it really is" refers to how a person actually looks, their real appearance. Hearing without obeying is like looking without doing anything about what one sees.

James, probably the brother of Jesus and a leader of the church in Jerusalem (as many understand it, though this is debated), writes to Christians who were scattered. He warns them that hearing teaching is not enough: they can deceive themselves into thinking they already obey, when they have only listened.

For today: after reading the Bible or hearing a sermon, choose one specific thing you can do this week, such as forgiving someone, helping a neighbor, or dropping a bad habit. Write it down and pray that you will follow through.
exp.0:23:
It says that the man looked at himself in the mirror, went away, and soon forgot what he looked like. "After observing himself" means that he took a close look at himself. "Goes away" means he walks off, and "what he looks like" refers to his appearance. The picture is of someone who sees his face but does not keep hold of what he saw.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to Christians to encourage them to live out what they believe. He compares someone who only hears the Word with someone who looks in the mirror and does nothing. The Word shows us how we are and what we need to change. Hearing it without acting on it is deceiving oneself.

For today: after reading the Bible or listening to a sermon, choose one concrete thing you can put into practice today, such as forgiving someone, being honest, or helping a person. Write it down and ask God for the strength to carry it out.
exp.0:1:
James says that when we run into all kinds of trials, we should consider them a reason for real joy.

"Consider" is the word James uses for seeing something in a certain light, and "pure joy" points to joy without mixture, joy that is whole and sincere. The trials he means are hardships that test faith, not only the pull toward doing wrong.

The writer is James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, and he speaks to believers scattered beyond their homeland. Many were facing pressure and suffering. The verses that follow explain the reason: tested faith produces endurance, and that endurance brings us to maturity. Scholars debate who this James is, though many think he is the brother of the Lord.

For today: the next time you face a difficulty, don't stop at asking "why me?" Ask God to use it to make you steadier, and remember that joy does not deny the pain, but trusts in God's purpose.
exp.2:12:
James asks who among you is wise and understanding. If someone is, let them show it through their good conduct, through deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom. The word "understanding" means insight or good judgment. "Conduct" here means behavior, the way a person lives, not just their speech. "Humility" means a modest and gentle attitude toward others.

James writes as a pastor to scattered Jewish Christians. He had just been speaking about the misuse of the tongue, which both blesses and curses. Now he moves from words to the whole of life. The verses that follow show that there was envy and quarreling among them, and that claiming to be wise was useless if the heart was full of bitterness.

For today: true wisdom is not measured by what we know or what we say, but by how we treat others. This week, when you face a disagreement, respond with calm and humility instead of trying to be right.
exp.1:20:
James asks whether our father Abraham was not declared righteous by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar. The word "justified" means declared righteous, approved before God.

James, leader of the church in Jerusalem, writes to Jewish believers scattered abroad. He corrects those who said they had faith but did not live according to it. Some think he contradicts Paul, who teaches that we are justified by faith. Many understand that Paul speaks of how the relationship with God begins, and James of how one shows that a faith is real. James himself points out that Abraham "believed God."

Today we might ask ourselves: does my faith show in what I do? This week, choose one concrete act of obedience or kindness that shows you are trusting God.
exp.0:14:
This verse says that evil desire works like a pregnancy: after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin, and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death. Desire here means an out-of-order craving for what God does not want. It is a process that moves from desire to sin to death.

James, whom tradition identifies as the brother of Jesus and a leader of the church in Jerusalem, writes to believers who were going through trials. Some could blame God for their falls. James makes clear that God tempts no one; the problem is born in the heart itself. He then reminds them that every good gift comes from God.

For today: do not wait for sin to be full-grown. When you notice a desire pushing you toward something harmful, deal with it early, pray honestly, and move away from whatever feeds it. Taking responsibility, without blaming God or others, opens the door to grace and to change.
exp.3:9:
He says we should humble ourselves before God, that is, acknowledge that we need him and that we are not self-sufficient. The word "exalt" in the verse means raise, honor, or set on high. The promise is that God himself will exalt us.

James, a leader of the church and, according to Christian tradition, a brother of the Lord, writes to believers who had quarrels, pride, and love for the world. Before this verse he calls them to draw near to God, leave sin behind, and repent sincerely. Afterward he rebukes them for speaking badly of one another and judging each other. Humility is the remedy for those divisions.

Today, if you have a conflict with someone, before defending yourself, pray and acknowledge your part before God. Then ask for forgiveness if it is needed. Let God be the one who exalts you, without having to win the argument.
exp.0:10:
The verse says that when the sun rises with its scorching heat, it withers the plant, its flower falls, and its beauty is lost. The same will happen to the rich man, who will fade away in the midst of his pursuits. "In the midst of his pursuits" refers to his business, his plans, and the way he lives his life. "Will fade away" means he will be gone, like a flower that has lost its life.

James, traditionally identified as the brother of Jesus, writes to Jewish believers scattered abroad who were going through trials. He reminds them that wealth is neither secure nor lasting. The poor person can rejoice in his worth before God, and the rich person should be humble, because we are all passing through.

Today we can ask ourselves what we are putting our security in. Money, work, or status can change quickly. It is worth living with humility and generosity, and placing our trust in God, whose love and promises do not wither.
exp.0:6:
This verse says that the person who doubts, who asks God but does not trust that he will answer, should not expect to receive anything from the Lord. The phrase "should not expect" here means "should not suppose" or "should not believe." "That man" refers to the one just described: the person who asks with doubt, like a wave tossed by the wind.

James, who is writing to Christians going through trials, has just said that God gives wisdom generously and without reproach. Now he contrasts that goodness with the attitude of the one who asks without confidence. The next verse calls him "double-minded," someone divided within. He is not speaking of someone who has questions or struggles with their faith, but of someone who will not settle into trusting God.

For today: when you ask God for direction, pray with sincerity and trust his good character. If you feel doubts, bring them honestly to him as well.
exp.1:12:
He says that God will judge without mercy the one who has not been merciful. But mercy triumphs over judgment, and it does so with joy.

James, a pastor of the church in Jerusalem, writes to Jewish believers who had been scattered. He has just rebuked them for treating the rich better than the poor. He reminds them that God's law is a whole, and that they will be judged by the law that gives freedom, the one kept through love rather than through mere obligation. Then he will say that true faith shows itself in deeds.

For today: think of someone who offended you or who needs help. Forgive them or help them this week with a concrete act of kindness. Whoever has received God's mercy shares it with others.
exp.0:17:
This verse says that God chose to give us new spiritual life through the gospel, the word of truth, and that no one forced him to do it. "Chose" tells us the gift came from his own decision. "Firstfruits" are the first part of the harvest, the portion set apart and offered to God as something special. So believers are like the beginning of what God intends to renew in his creation.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to Christians who were going through trials. Earlier he spoke about God giving only good things and never changing. Here he shows that the greatest of those gifts is our new life in Christ. Then he goes on to speak about listening more and getting angry less.

For today: if your new life was a gift from God, live it with gratitude and humility. Today, before you react in anger, stop and listen first.
exp.1:10:
This verse says the law comes from one God. The same God who said "Do not commit adultery" also said "Do not murder." So if someone did not commit adultery but did commit murder, they have still broken the law.

James, a leader in the early church, writes to believers who treated the rich better than the poor. He explains that this favoritism is a serious sin. You cannot choose which commandments to keep and think everything is fine, because the law is a unity and comes from the authority of God.

For today: do not compare yourself to others by saying "I don't do such things." Examine your attitudes as well, such as contempt or favoritism, and ask God for a merciful heart, because all of us need his forgiveness.
exp.2:0:
James says that not many of you should become teachers. The Berean Standard Bible puts it plainly: "Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, because you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly." The idea is that the one who teaches will be judged by God with greater seriousness.

The speaker is James, who writes to believers he calls "my brothers." The verses that follow speak about the power of the tongue: we all stumble in speech, and words can guide or harm, like a bridle on a horse. That is why teaching is a great responsibility. Scholars debate exactly which group of teachers he had in mind, and it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: before advising, correcting, or teaching others, ask yourself whether you live it first, and speak with humility, care, and truth. Teaching is not wrong, but it calls for seriousness.
exp.0:3:
It says we should let perseverance (the steadiness to stay firm in the middle of trials) finish its work in us. The result is that we become "mature and complete," that is, lacking nothing important in our character.

James, a leader of the church and brother of the Lord according to Christian tradition, writes to believers who were going through hardship. Earlier he said that the testing of faith produces perseverance. Now he explains what it is for: to mature. Right after this he speaks about asking God for wisdom.

For today: when you go through a difficult moment, do not rush to get out of it as quickly as possible. Ask God for help to endure with faith, trusting that He is forming something good in you.
exp.0:7:
This verse says that a person who is double-minded is not steady in anything he does. The Berean Standard Bible begins with "He is a double-minded man," and the phrase means having two minds, or a divided heart. "Unstable" means that he changes often and does not hold firm. "Ways" refers to the way he lives and makes decisions.

James writes as a pastor to Christians who were going through trials. He has just said that whoever asks God for wisdom must ask in faith. He compares the one who doubts to a wave moved by the wind. Here he explains the root of the problem: someone who wants to trust God, but who also leans his heart on other things.

For today: when you pray or make a decision, ask yourself whether you truly trust God or whether you keep a backup option in your heart. Tell him honestly, "Lord, help me to trust you completely." He welcomes those who come with humility.
exp.1:1:
This verse begins to give a concrete example. A wealthy man comes into the meeting, wearing a gold ring and fine clothing, and a poor man also comes in, wearing shabby clothes. The word translated "meeting" here can also mean "synagogue," the place where people gather. In this context, "shabby" describes clothing that is worn, dirty, or of little value.

James, a leader of the church and perhaps the brother of Jesus (as most think), writes to scattered Jewish Christians. He warns them against favoritism, because faith in the glorious Jesus does not allow treating some people better than others according to their money or position.

For today: when someone new arrives at your church, workplace, or group, greet them with the same warmth, without looking at their clothing, their bank account, or their appearance. Ask yourself whether you give everyone the same attention.
exp.3:8:
This verse calls for real sorrow over sin. The words "Grieve, mourn, and weep" call for sorrow that is felt deeply and shown openly. The laughter and joy mentioned here are not just any happiness, but the lightness of someone who lives as if sin doesn't matter. James asks that this attitude be replaced with seriousness and repentance.

James, who according to tradition is the brother of the Lord, writes to Christians who were fighting among themselves and who mixed their love for God with love for the world. Before this verse he calls them to submit to God and to purify their hearts. Afterward he invites them to humble themselves so that God may lift them up.

Today we can take a moment to pray and honestly acknowledge where we have fallen short, without excuses or mockery. That sincere sorrow does not crush us; it is the step that opens the door to the forgiveness and restoration God promises.
exp.4:6:
It says that believers should be patient until the Lord returns. James uses the example of the farmer: he plants and then waits for the precious fruit of the soil. The fall and spring rains are what help the crop grow and ripen. "Be patient" means to endure calmly, without giving up.

James writes to scattered Jewish Christians, many of them poor and mistreated. Earlier he had rebuked the rich who exploited them. Now he encourages the oppressed not to take revenge or despair, because God sees and will judge with justice. The exact timing of Christ's return is not detailed here.

For today: when an unjust or difficult situation drags on, do not retaliate or fill yourself with bitterness. Pray, keep doing good, and trust that God works in his own time, as the farmer trusts the rain.
exp.4:10:
