This verse says that we count those blessed who keep enduring hardship with steady faithfulness. The word translated "blessed" here means happy or fortunate. "Perseverance" means steady endurance under trial. James points back to Job and to the outcome the Lord brought about for him. That outcome shows that the Lord is full of compassion and mercy.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to believers who were suffering injustice and were tempted to complain against one another. He asks them to wait for the coming of the Lord and gives them examples: the prophets and Job. Some understand "the outcome from the Lord" as what God did for Job; others understand it as the outcome of Jesus on the cross and the resurrection. Both readings are discussed.

When you go through a trial, do not stay fixed on the pain of the moment. Remember that God is compassionate and that there is an outcome. Endure without taking it out on others, and pray.
exp.4:17:
It says that Elijah prayed again and God answered: the heavens gave rain and the earth yielded its crops once more. The word "crops" here refers to what the earth produces, such as grain and food. After the drought, Elijah's prayer opened the way for the rain.

James, a leader in the church, writes to believers who were going through hard times. He teaches them that the prayer of a righteous person has great power. He holds up Elijah as an example, and he stresses that Elijah was an ordinary man, with the same weaknesses we have. Elijah's story appears in 1 Kings 17 and 18.

For today: you do not need to be perfect or famous to pray. Pray with faith and persistence for your own needs and for the needs of others, and trust that God hears. He decides how and when to answer, but he invites his people to pray.
exp.4:16:
James says that Elijah was an ordinary man, just like us. The phrase "subject to like passions" does not mean something bad. It means that he felt, struggled and grew tired just like anyone else. Even so, he prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three and a half years.

The one speaking is James, a leader of the early church, writing to believers who were facing hardships. He has just said that "the effective, fervent prayer of a righteous man avails much," and now he gives an example from the Old Testament (1 Kings 17 and 18). Elijah was not special for being perfect, but because he prayed in faith.

For today: do not think your prayer is worth little because you feel weak or ordinary. Pray with confidence about that specific need; God hears people like you.
exp.2:9:
It says that out of the same mouth come good words and bad words. James calls the believers "brothers" and tells them that this should not be, meaning that this is not right, it is not what ought to happen. The words "blessing" and "cursing" refer to speaking well or badly about someone.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to Christians and speaks of how hard it is to control the tongue. He has just said that with it we praise God and also hurt people made in his image. Then he uses examples from nature: a spring does not give sweet water and bitter water at the same time.

Today, before you speak, think about whether your words honor God and value the person who hears you or the person you are talking about. If you fail, ask God for help and ask forgiveness from the person you offended.
exp.4:7:
James tells his readers to be patient, just as a farmer waits for his crop. He asks them to strengthen their hearts and keep them steady. The reason is that the Lord's coming is near.

James writes to believers who were suffering unfairness, especially at the hands of rich and powerful people who oppressed them. He encourages them not to take revenge, but to wait steadily for the return of Christ, who will bring justice. The examples of the farmer and the prophets show that patient waiting is part of faith.

When something wears you down or treats you unfairly, do not let yourself be carried away by despair or anger. Each day, do something concrete to strengthen your heart: pray, read the Bible, and trust that God is at work, even when you cannot yet see it.
exp.3:12:
James calls out those who speak with great confidence about their plans. Everything sounds very firm and well calculated.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to scattered Jewish Christians. Earlier he spoke to them about not judging one another. Now he turns to another kind of pride: making plans as if one controlled the future. He does not condemn planning or working, but forgetting God and boasting. The verses that follow make this clear.

Today we can make plans, but with humility. Before deciding something important, let us pray and say from the heart: "Lord, if you will." In this way we trust God and not our own control.
exp.1:2:
Here James continues with the example of two men who come to the gathering. He says that if you lavish attention on the man in fine clothes and say, "Here is a seat of honor," but say to the poor man, "You must stand," or "Sit at my feet," you are doing wrong.

The phrase "sit at my feet" refers to sitting on the floor beside a low stool where a person rested their feet.

James, a leader of the church and, according to tradition, the brother of the Lord, writes to Jewish believers scattered abroad. He corrects them because they were giving more honor to the rich than to the poor, something that contradicts faith in Christ.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we treat everyone equally in the church and outside it. This week, greet and attend to a humble person with the same warmth you show someone with more money or influence.
exp.4:1:
This verse says that the riches of the rich have already rotted, like food gone bad. Their fine clothes, which once showed their wealth, have been eaten through by moths. "Rotted" means spoiled and worthless; the moth is the insect that chews holes in cloth.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to scattered believers. Here he speaks sharply to wealthy people who hoarded their goods and did not pay fair wages to their workers, as the following verses say. Many understand them to be unjust rich people, not necessarily members of the church. It is a warning of judgment.

For today: examine how you use your possessions. Pay fairly those who work for you, be generous, and do not place your security in what passes away, but in God.
exp.2:14:
It says that the "wisdom" of someone who lives with bitter envy and a desire to fight does not come from God. It is "earthly," belonging to this world; "unspiritual," following instincts and not the Spirit; and "demonic," resembling the way of thinking of God's enemy. "Unspiritual" here does not refer to beasts, but to what is unguided by the Spirit.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to believers who considered themselves wise, but who lived with rivalries and pride. He tells them that true wisdom is shown by good conduct and gentleness, not by words or by boasting. He then contrasts this false wisdom with the wisdom that comes from above.

For today: when you feel envy or want to win an argument at any cost, stop and ask yourself where that "reasoning" comes from. Ask God for a humble and peaceful heart, and respond with gentleness.
exp.2:3:
This verse says that ships, even though they are huge and driven by strong winds, are steered by a very small rudder. The pilot moves it wherever he is inclined, and the ship follows. The phrase "strong winds" in this verse refers to forces that push hard against the vessel, and "wherever the pilot is inclined" means wherever the pilot chooses to go.

James, whom tradition identifies with the Lord's brother and leader of the church in Jerusalem, writes to Jewish believers scattered abroad. He is speaking about the power of the tongue. After the image of the horse's bit, he uses the rudder as a second picture: something small can direct something large. His aim is to show that words, though they may seem like little things, guide a whole life.

Today, before you answer in anger or repeat a piece of gossip, take a short pause and ask God to guide your words. One well-chosen sentence can change the course of a conversation, a family, or a friendship.
exp.1:13:
James asks what good it is if someone says they have faith but their life does not show it. The final question, "Can such faith save him?", expects the answer "no": a faith that is only in words does not save. "Good" here means "help" or "use," and "deeds" are the actions that come from believing.

James, probably the brother of the Lord and a leader of the church in Jerusalem, writes to Jewish Christians scattered abroad. He had been speaking about mercy and judgment. His concern is that some accepted the teaching but ignored those in need, as the example that follows of the brother without clothing or food shows.

For today: if you see a need near you, do not stop at good wishes or at saying "I will pray for you." Pray, and also take a concrete step: bring food, offer your time, or help with something practical. In this way your faith becomes visible.
exp.0:26:
James says that the religion God regards as pure and clean shows itself in two things: caring for orphans and widows when they are suffering, and keeping oneself from being polluted by the world. "Care for" here means going to help, not just paying a brief call. "Polluted" means being marked or dirtied. "The world" refers to the system of values that turns away from God.

The writer is James, who presents himself as a servant of God and of Jesus Christ (it is traditionally thought he was the Lord's brother). He writes to believers and insists that faith must show itself in actions. Earlier he spoke about being doers of the word and about controlling the tongue. In that time, orphans and widows often had no protection or means of support.

Today you could look for a person or family who is alone or in need, and help them in a concrete way: by spending time with them, bringing food, or supporting them with a practical matter. Let your faith be seen in your love.
exp.0:5:
It says that when we ask God for wisdom, we should ask with confidence, without doubting Him. "Without doubting" means not doubting at all. Whoever doubts is like a wave of the sea that the wind blows and tosses, with no fixed direction.

"Upbraideth," in the verse before, means to reproach or throw something in someone's face.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to believers who were going through trials. He tells them that patience matures them and that, if they lack wisdom to face those difficulties, God gives it generously. Here he warns against the attitude of someone who asks but does not truly trust God. Some understand that he is referring to constant doubt, not to a moment of weakness.

Today: when you face a difficult decision, ask God for wisdom simply and trust that He is good. If doubts overwhelm you, tell them to Him in prayer and choose to keep trusting in His generous character.
exp.1:19:
James asks someone who boasts of having faith: "O foolish man, do you want evidence that faith without deeds is worthless?" The word "foolish" describes someone who talks a lot but has nothing real to show for it. The word "worthless" means it does not produce anything good or useful.

James, a leader of the early church, writes to believers and corrects those who said they believed in God but did not help anyone or live differently. Earlier he reminded his readers that even the demons believe that God exists, and yet they tremble. Believing only in the mind is not enough. Some interpreters see a clash here with Paul, but many think they are speaking of the same thing from different angles: true faith shows itself in life.

Today, do not be satisfied with simply saying "I believe." Ask God what concrete act of love you can do this week, such as helping a needy neighbor or forgiving someone, so that your faith becomes visible.
exp.4:3:
He says that the wages of the workers who mowed the rich people's fields were withheld from them. That unpaid money is crying out against them, as if it had a voice, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts. The "wages" are the payment for a day's work, "mowed" means cutting down the harvest, and "Lord of Hosts" is a title that speaks of God as the Sovereign over all power.

James writes to scattered Christians and denounces the rich who pile up wealth at the expense of the poor. Earlier he showed that their gold and clothing are rotting, and then he accuses them of living in luxury. In doing this, James follows the tradition of the prophets, who taught that God hears the oppressed.

For today: if you have employees or pay for a service, pay them in full and on time. If you work for someone else, remember that God sees injustice and hears your cry.

sum.2: James warns that the tongue, though small, has great power to guide or to destroy, like a bit in a horse's mouth or a rudder on a ship, and no one can tame it on their own. It is inconsistent to bless God and then curse people. That is why true wisdom shows itself in gentleness, peace, and mercy, not in envy or quarreling.
sum.0: James encourages believers to see trials as an occasion for joy, because they produce patience, and to ask God for wisdom in faith. He explains that God gives good gifts and tempts no one, since sin arises from one's own desire. He closes by calling people to listen well, control their tongue, and obey the Word, caring for orphans and widows.
sum.1: James asks believers not to treat the rich person better than the poor one, because God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith, and loving one's neighbor is the royal law. He then teaches that faith without works is dead, and he gives Abraham and Rahab as examples.
sum.4: James warns the rich who exploit their workers, and calls believers to be patient until the Lord returns, like the farmer who waits for the crops and like the prophets. He encourages them to speak the truth, to pray in every situation, to confess their sins to one another, and to help anyone who wanders away from the faith.
sum.3: James explains that quarrels arise from selfish desires, and that we ask wrongly when we seek only pleasure. He calls us to give up friendship with the world, submit to God, resist the devil, and humble ourselves. He also warns us not to judge a brother and not to boast about the future, because life is brief and everything depends on God.
